description: We are agCoders, a team joining the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in Yangon. We love technology, coding, and solving real-world problems. Our project aims to help farmers and researchers make better decisions using NASA satellite data.
summary:
Green Ally is a farmer-centered decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps farmers answer a practical question: “What should I plant after this harvest, and what risks should I consider?”

As rainfall becomes less predictable and drought, floods, heat, and soil degradation threaten livelihoods, farmers need guidance they can act on—not just satellite maps.

Green Ally combines NASA Earth observations, historical weather, soil conditions, crop requirements, and farmers' priorities to compare multi-season crop rotations.

Using daily weather records from 2016–2025, the platform evaluates water demand, flood and temperature exposure, erosion risk, soil health, disease carryover, and potential income.

Its key innovation is explainable, climate-aware decision-making. It shows how NASA data influences crop comparisons, explains trade-offs in plain language, and highlights uncertain or missing evidence.

Initially focused on Myanmar's Ayeyarwady Delta, Central Dry Zone, and Shan uplands, Green Ally aims to transform complex Earth science into practical farming decisions that support local knowledge and build climate resilience.
details:
Green Ally is a farmer-centered crop-rotation decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps farmers explore what to plant next by comparing possible crop sequences with local soil information, crop characteristics, field history, farmer priorities, and available NASA Earth observations. The project’s pilot context is Myanmar, including the Ayeyarwady Delta, Central Dry Zone, and Shan uplands.

Source Code: github.com/wintkhantlin/green-ally
Website: greenally.vercel.app

Features

  • NASA data that can change the decision: Environmental evidence is connected to crop-rotation comparisons, so water and climate constraints can affect which options appear more suitable—not just decorate a map.
  • Whole rotations, not one-crop guesses: Compare sequences such as monsoon rice followed by black gram against alternatives, while considering how one crop may affect the next.
  • Replay against ten years of historical weather: Examine how candidate rotations line up with past seasons, including rainfall shortfalls, dry spells, and temperature exposure. This is a historical comparison, not a forecast.
  • See the trade-offs behind each option: Explore considerations such as water use, soil and crop-family context, risks, and available income evidence instead of receiving an unexplained “best crop.”
  • A transparent “unknown” when evidence is missing: If a source is unavailable, too coarse, or insufficient for a field-level conclusion, the platform can show that limitation instead of quietly treating missing data as a favorable result.
  • Know what the satellite can actually see: Source dates, coverage, and spatial scale help distinguish field imagery from broader regional context.
  • Plan for farmer priorities: Compare options in light of priorities such as water conservation, crop diversity, legume inclusion, living cover, and income—and see when the available evidence cannot yet assess a priority.
  • Turn analysis into a practical discussion: Explanations, cautions, and missing-information prompts help farmers and agricultural advisers identify what to check locally before acting.
  • Crop rotation comparison: Compares sequences across multiple seasons rather than recommending a single crop in isolation. It considers crop calendars, growing periods, soil pH, drainage, temperature ranges, crop-family repetition, and the farmer’s accessible crops.
  • Historical weather replay: Reviews candidate rotations against historical weather to highlight rainfall shortfalls, dry spells, and temperature exposure. It helps users compare options under past conditions; it does not predict next year’s weather.
  • Water-risk screening: Considers rainfall, crop water demand, and soil-water information when available. It can assess whether post-rice conditions may be suitable for establishing a following crop, while showing when missing soil-moisture data limits the assessment.
  • Flood-exposure screening: Uses available clear satellite imagery to identify observed open water. It shows observation coverage and dates, while communicating that clouds, image gaps, and the limits of optical imagery can prevent a reliable assessment.
  • Heat and cold screening: Checks whether temperatures in the supplied environmental data fall outside a crop’s known temperature ranges. These checks are screening indicators, not predictions of crop damage.
  • Erosion-exposure screening: Considers slope, seasonal rainfall, and periods when the field may have little crop cover to flag conditions that may deserve local review.
  • Soil and rotation context: Uses soil estimates and crop information to examine factors such as pH, drainage, crop-family diversity, legume inclusion, and residue management. It does not claim measured improvements in soil health or guaranteed pest control.
  • Farmer-priority comparison: Lets the decision process reflect priorities such as water conservation, crop diversity, legume inclusion, living cover, and income. It makes clear when a priority cannot be evaluated with the available evidence.
  • Income-range comparison: Can compare estimated gross-margin ranges using available yield, price, and variable-cost information. It can also show break-even prices and identify when financial impacts cannot be reliably quantified.
  • Explainable results: Provides reasons, cautions, missing information, and evidence details to help farmers understand why options differ and what to check before acting. The first-listed option is not automatically treated as the winner.
  • Evidence and uncertainty display: Shows source, observation period, spatial scale, and data limitations where available. Unknown or unavailable data is identified as missing instead of being treated as zero or as evidence of safety.
  • Field and regional context: Uses satellite and environmental information at its appropriate scale, distinguishing field-level imagery from broader regional or surrounding-area data.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project aims to make Earth-observation data easier to interpret for practical farm-planning discussions. By comparing water, climate, soil, and economic considerations together, it can help farmers and agricultural advisers identify trade-offs, discuss possible vulnerabilities, and decide what additional local information to gather. Its intended impact is to support more informed crop-rotation planning and long-term farm resilience, especially in regions facing changing rainfall, heat, water constraints, and soil challenges.

Tools and Data

The application is built with TypeScript and Next.js, with a crop-rotation engine that evaluates candidate sequences and presents explanations and cautions. The project uses or is designed to work with NASA sources including NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, Landsat/HLS, ECOSTRESS, and SRTM. It also incorporates soil estimates from ISRIC SoilGrids, crop information, and regional agricultural references.

What Makes It Creative

Green Ally connects environmental evidence to the rotation decision itself. Instead of placing satellite maps beside a generic crop suggestion, it compares whole crop sequences, exposes the trade-offs behind them, and shows when evidence is too limited to make a confident comparison. The team considered farmers’ priorities, Myanmar’s varied growing regions, data coverage and resolution, scientific uncertainty, and the need to present technical evidence in clear, practical language.
